notes.h: How human activity upsets coastal processes
notes.b: Coasts are a balance between erosion, transport and deposition, and human activity can upset that balance.
points: Human activity can interrupt longshore drift, remove sediment, destroy the vegetation that holds dunes together, or reflect wave energy.
The effects often appear further along the coast, downdrift, rather than where the work was done.

notes.h: Trampling, vehicles and blowouts on dunes
points: Trampling of sand dunes by walkers and sunbathers kills marram grass.
With no roots binding it, the sand is removed by the wind, cutting blowouts (hollows) into the dunes.
A blowout can breach the dune ridge, letting the sea reach the land behind.
Vehicles and parking on dunes and beaches destroy vegetation and compact the sand; caravan parks and holiday homes built on dunes do the same.

notes.h: Golf courses, footpaths and busy viewpoints
points: Golf courses on dunes (links) stabilise some dunes, but replace natural habitats and lead to demands for defences to protect the course.
Footpath erosion and cliff-edge damage occur at busy viewing points.
Litter, pollution and disturbance of nesting and feeding birds follow heavy use.
Hotels, apartments and promenades built on the beach or dune line remove the natural sediment store.
They block the natural landward movement of dunes and beaches, so the beach narrows and defences become necessary; this is called coastal squeeze.
Example: the Spanish Mediterranean coast, including the Costa del Sol and Benidorm on the Costa Blanca, where high-rise resorts have been built along the shore since mass tourism grew in the 1960s.
Hard engineering builds structures to resist the sea; soft engineering works with natural processes.
Hard engineering is usually expensive and effective locally, and it can increase erosion elsewhere.

notes.b: A sea wall protects the land behind it but changes the processes in front of it.
points: Sea walls are concrete or stone walls, often curved (recurved) to throw waves back.
They reflect wave energy, so backwash scours the beach in front, lowering and narrowing it, and the wall itself is undermined.
Erosion often increases at the ends of a sea wall.
Sea walls are expensive to build and maintain.
Rock armour (rip-rap) is large boulders piled at the foot of a cliff or in front of a sea wall.
The gaps between the boulders absorb and break up wave energy.
It is cheaper than a sea wall and quick to place.
It can be unsightly and hard to walk over, and big storms may move the boulders.
In photographs, rock armour appears as a pile of loose boulders at the cliff foot or wall.
Groynes are low wooden, rock or concrete barriers built out from the shore at right angles, across the beach.
They trap sand moving by longshore drift on their updrift side, widening the beach, which absorbs wave energy.
Effect on processes: the beach downdrift is starved of sediment, so erosion increases there.
Unlike rock armour, which lies along the foot of a cliff or wall, groynes run out across the beach at right angles to the shore.
Gabions are wire cages filled with stones.
Revetments are sloping wooden, concrete or rock structures that break waves.
Offshore breakwaters and reefs are structures parallel to the shore, just offshore, that make waves break before they reach the beach.
Training walls and harbour piers interrupt longshore drift and cause deposition in new places; the North Bull Wall, Dublin Bay, is an example.
Beach nourishment pumps or trucks sand or shingle onto a beach to widen it.
It looks natural and keeps the beach for tourism.
It must be repeated, as waves remove the sand, and dredging the source can harm the sea bed.
Dune regeneration uses sand fencing or brushwood to trap blown sand, replants marram grass, and fences off damaged areas.
It is cheap and natural, but takes years and needs visitors to keep off the dunes.
In managed retreat (managed realignment), or 'do nothing', defences are removed or not replaced, and the sea is allowed to flood low-value land.
The flooded land becomes salt marsh, which absorbs wave energy and provides habitat.
It is cheap and sustainable, but landowners lose land.

notes.h: Case study: Mappleton, Holderness coast, England
notes.b: The Mappleton scheme shows how a defence can move erosion downdrift.
points: At Mappleton, on the Holderness coast, England, a 1991 scheme of two rock groynes and rock armour at the cliff foot protected the village and the main coast road.
The scheme cost about £2 million.
Result: the beach built up between the groynes, but the cliffs immediately south of the scheme, starved of sediment, eroded faster than before.
This is the textbook example of defence moving the problem downdrift.

notes.h: Case study: North Bull Island, Dublin Bay
points: The North Bull Wall was built in the 1820s to stop sand silting up the entrance to Dublin Port.
Sand then built up against and beside the wall, and North Bull Island grew from a sandbank into an island with dunes, salt marsh and mudflats.
It is an example of a human structure causing deposition.

notes.h: Case study: Rosslare Strand, Co. Wexford
points: Rosslare Strand is a sandy resort coast on an eroding shoreline.
It is protected by groynes and rock armour.

notes.b: After the 1953 storm surge, the Dutch built defences that were balanced with conservation.
points: The North Sea storm surge of 1953 flooded the south-west of the Netherlands and killed about 1,800 people there.
The response was the Delta Works: dams, sluices and storm-surge barriers that shortened and sealed the coast of Zeeland.
The Oosterschelde (Eastern Scheldt) barrier, completed in 1986, has movable gates that stay open in normal weather.
Because the tides still flow in, the estuary's ecosystem and shellfish industry are kept, which makes this defence balanced with conservation.
Coasts are under pressure from erosion, development, tourism and rising sea levels.
Management tries to protect people and property while keeping natural processes and habitats working.
Integrated coastal zone management (ICZM) plans a whole stretch of coast, a sediment cell, as one unit.
ICZM balances defence, tourism, development and conservation, because work in one place affects places downdrift.

notes.h: Legal protection and the Blue Flag
points: The EU Habitats and Birds Directives protect coastal sites through Special Areas of Conservation (SACs) for habitats and Special Protection Areas (SPAs) for birds, which together form the Natura 2000 network.
In Ireland, the National Parks and Wildlife Service oversees these sites.
Planning controls restrict building close to the shore.
Spain's Ley de Costas (Coastal Law) of 1988 was passed in response to overdevelopment and restricts building on the shore zone.
Blue Flag is an international beach award run by the Foundation for Environmental Education and administered in Ireland by An Taisce.
Its criteria cover water quality, environmental education and information, environmental management, and safety and services, encouraging councils to manage beaches well.
Dune management at busy beaches uses boardwalks and marked paths, fencing off eroded areas, marram replanting, moving car parks back from the dunes, information signs and seasonal wardens.

Example: Brittas Bay, Co. Wicklow, is a dune system heavily used by day-trippers from Dublin in summer; trampling and parking damaged the dunes, which are part of a protected Special Area of Conservation.
Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare: a visitor centre, built into the hillside, opened in 2007.
Paths and a wall or barrier are set back from the cliff edge to control trampling and keep people safe.

notes.h: North Bull Island as a conservation site
points: North Bull Island, Dublin Bay, has been a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve since 1981, and was extended in 2015 as the Dublin Bay Biosphere.
Its salt marsh and mudflats are a major wintering ground for Brent geese and other wildfowl and waders.
Pressures include the Royal Dublin and St Anne's golf courses on the island, cars driving onto the beach, and many visitors from the city.
It shows recreation, conservation and a human-made landform in one place.
Medmerry, West Sussex, England, was completed in 2013 as a managed realignment scheme.
The shingle bank was no longer maintained, a new embankment was built further inland, and the sea was let in to create intertidal habitat.
This intertidal habitat absorbs wave energy.
Hard defences protect a place, but they move erosion downdrift and are costly.
Soft measures are cheaper and more sustainable, but slower and less certain.
The best management works with the sediment system along a whole coast.

factCards.term: Human activity on coasts: four ways it upsets coastal processes
factCards.definition: It interrupts longshore drift; removes sediment; destroys the vegetation that holds dunes together; reflects wave energy. The effects often appear further along the coast, downdrift, rather than where the work was done.

factCards.term: Trampling of sand dunes: how it leads to blowouts
factCards.definition: Walkers and sunbathers kill the marram grass; with no roots binding it, wind removes the sand and cuts blowouts into the dunes; a blowout can breach the dune ridge and let the sea reach the land behind.

factCards.term: Recreation: other pressures on dunes, cliffs and birds
factCards.definition: Vehicles, parking, caravan parks and holiday homes on dunes kill plants and compact sand; golf links stabilise some dunes but replace habitats and bring demands for defences; footpath and cliff-edge erosion at busy viewpoints; litter and disturbance of birds.

factCards.term: Spanish Mediterranean coast: how resorts caused coastal squeeze

factCards.term: Ley de Costas, 1988: what Spain did and why
factCards.definition: Spain passed its Coastal Law (Ley de Costas) in 1988 in response to overdevelopment; it restricts building on the shore zone.

factCards.term: Hard vs soft engineering: how they differ in approach and effect
factCards.definition: Hard engineering builds structures to resist the sea; it is usually expensive, effective locally, and can increase erosion elsewhere. Soft engineering works with natural processes; it is cheaper and more sustainable, but slower and less certain.

factCards.term: Sea walls: how they work, their effects on the coast and their cost
factCards.definition: Often curved to throw waves back, they protect the land behind but reflect wave energy, so backwash scours the beach in front, lowering it and undermining the wall; erosion often increases at its ends. They are expensive to build and maintain.

factCards.term: Rock armour: how it works, two advantages and three disadvantages
factCards.definition: Large boulders are piled at the foot of a cliff or in front of a sea wall, and the gaps absorb and break up wave energy. It is cheaper than a sea wall and quick to place, but it can be unsightly and hard to walk over, and big storms may move the boulders.

factCards.term: Groynes: effect on longshore drift updrift and downdrift
factCards.definition: Built across the beach at right angles to the shore, groynes trap sand moving by longshore drift on their updrift side, widening the beach so it absorbs wave energy; downdrift, the beach is starved of sediment and erosion increases.

factCards.term: Rock armour vs groynes: how to tell them apart in a photo
factCards.definition: Rock armour is a pile of loose boulders lying along the foot of a cliff or wall. Groynes are low barriers running out across the beach at right angles to the shore. Rosslare Strand, Co. Wexford, an eroding sandy resort coast, is protected by both.

factCards.term: Beach nourishment and dune regeneration: pros and cons
factCards.definition: Nourishment widens a beach with sand or shingle: it looks natural and keeps the beach for tourism, but must be repeated, and dredging can harm the sea bed. Dune regeneration (sand fencing, marram replanting, fencing off): cheap and natural, but slow.

factCards.term: Managed retreat: how it works, with an example
factCards.definition: Defences are removed or not replaced and the sea floods low-value land, creating salt marsh that absorbs wave energy and gives habitat: cheap and sustainable, but landowners lose land. Medmerry, West Sussex (2013): a new embankment inland, the sea let in.

factCards.term: North Bull Wall: how a human structure created North Bull Island
factCards.definition: The North Bull Wall was built in the 1820s to stop sand silting up the entrance to Dublin Port. Sand built up against and beside it, and North Bull Island grew from a sandbank into an island with dunes, salt marsh and mudflats.

factCards.term: Netherlands, 1953: the flood and the Delta Works
factCards.definition: The 1953 North Sea storm surge flooded the south-west of the Netherlands and killed about 1,800 people there. The Delta Works followed: dams, sluices and storm-surge barriers that shortened and sealed the coast of Zeeland.

factCards.term: Oosterschelde barrier: why it balances defence with conservation
factCards.definition: Completed in 1986, this storm-surge barrier has movable gates that stay open in normal weather, so the tides still flow in and the estuary's ecosystem and shellfish industry are kept.

factCards.term: ICZM: why a whole sediment cell is managed as one unit
factCards.definition: Work in one place affects places downdrift, so integrated coastal zone management plans a whole stretch of coast together, balancing defence, tourism, development and conservation.

factCards.term: Legal protection of coasts: EU and Irish measures
factCards.definition: The EU Habitats and Birds Directives create Special Areas of Conservation and Special Protection Areas (birds), forming the Natura 2000 network, overseen in Ireland by the National Parks and Wildlife Service. Planning controls limit building near the shore.

factCards.definition: Run by the Foundation for Environmental Education and administered in Ireland by An Taisce. Criteria: water quality; environmental education and information; environmental management; safety and services. It encourages councils to manage beaches well.

factCards.term: Brittas Bay, Co. Wicklow: the pressures and how they are managed
factCards.definition: A dune system heavily used by day-trippers from Dublin in summer; trampling and parking damaged the dunes, part of a protected Special Area of Conservation. Managed with fencing, boardwalks and car parks set back from the dunes.

factCards.term: Cliffs of Moher: how a busy cliff site is managed
factCards.definition: A visitor centre built into the hillside opened in 2007; paths and a wall or barrier set back from the cliff edge control trampling and keep people safe.

factCards.term: North Bull Island as a conservation site: designations and pressures
factCards.definition: A UNESCO Biosphere Reserve since 1981, extended in 2015 as the Dublin Bay Biosphere; its salt marsh and mudflats are a major wintering ground for Brent geese. Pressures: the Royal Dublin and St Anne's golf courses, cars on the beach and many visitors.

questions.prompt: Examine the impact of coastal defence measures on coastal processes, with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: Sea walls reflect wave energy, so backwash scours the beach in front, lowering and narrowing it, and erosion often increases at the ends of the wall. Rock armour lies at the foot of a cliff or wall, and the gaps between its boulders absorb and break up wave energy, which protects the cliff foot. Groynes run out across the beach at right angles to the shore; they trap sand moving by longshore drift on their updrift side, widening the beach, but the beach downdrift is starved of sediment, so erosion increases there. At Mappleton on the Holderness coast, England, a 1991 scheme of two rock groynes and rock armour protected the village and the main coast road. The beach built up between the groynes, but the cliffs immediately south of the scheme, starved of sediment, eroded faster than before. The North Bull Wall, built in the 1820s to stop sand silting up Dublin Port, changed deposition in Dublin Bay: sand built up beside it and North Bull Island grew from a sandbank. Evaluation: hard defences protect a place but move erosion downdrift and are costly. Soft measures such as managed realignment are cheaper and more sustainable, but slower and less certain.

questions.prompt: Human activities can impact on the operation of coastal processes. Examine this statement with reference to recreational pressures and to conservation and management measures.
questions.model: Human activity can upset the balance between erosion, transport and deposition. Trampling of dunes by walkers and sunbathers kills marram grass; with no roots binding the sand, the wind cuts blowouts, and a blowout can breach the dune ridge and let the sea reach the land behind. Resort development on the Spanish Mediterranean coast, such as Benidorm on the Costa Blanca, has built hotels and apartments on the beach and dune line, removing the sediment store and blocking the landward movement of dunes and beaches; the beach narrows and defences become necessary, which is coastal squeeze. Dune management at Brittas Bay, Co. Wicklow, uses boardwalks, fencing, marram replanting and car parks set back from the dunes, and the dunes are part of a Special Area of Conservation. Blue Flag beaches, administered in Ireland by An Taisce, are judged on water quality and management, which encourages councils to manage beaches well. The Natura 2000 network of SACs and SPAs, and planning controls on building near the shore, limit development. North Bull Island, Dublin Bay, has been a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve since 1981, and its salt marsh and mudflats support Brent geese; golf courses, cars on the beach and city visitors put pressure on it. Recreation damages dunes, and conservation tries to limit that impact while keeping the coast working.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between rock armour and groynes.
questions.model: Rock armour is a layer of large boulders piled along the foot of a cliff or in front of a sea wall; the gaps between the boulders absorb and break up wave energy. Its disadvantage is that it can be unsightly and hard to walk over. Groynes are low barriers built out from the shore at right angles, across the beach; they trap sand on their updrift side. Their disadvantage is that the beach downdrift is starved of sediment, so erosion increases there.
